name: Riverside Avondale
title: Artificial Turf in Riverside Avondale, FL | TIMELESS Grass & Greens
description: Artificial turf, pet runs and putting greens in Riverside Avondale, and what the historic district review means for your yard before any work starts.
h1: Artificial turf in Riverside Avondale, FL, for homes in the historic district.
lede: In Riverside Avondale, the back yard is usually the easier place for a lawn or dog run. We measure at a free visit and draw a layout you approve.
wins: A drawn layout to send the City before work starts
Back-yard turf planned out of the street's view
A base matched to your end of the district

answer.question: Do I need a Certificate of Appropriateness for artificial turf in Riverside Avondale?
answer.answer: Possibly, and the City gives the answer. Jacksonville requires a Certificate of Appropriateness before any alteration in the historic district, but exempts routine lawn care unless it adds hardscape, and the code doesn't say which side of that line turf falls on.

blocks.h2: Ask which review your turf needs before the old lawn comes up.
blocks.takeaway: Any alteration in the historic district needs a Certificate of Appropriateness on top of any permit, though routine lawn care is exempt. Ask the City's Historic Preservation Section whether your turf layout needs one.
paras: Riverside and Avondale share one City historic district. Jacksonville's code requires a Certificate of Appropriateness, on top of any permit, before any alteration affecting property in it, and work started without one can be stopped with a notice of violation (Ord. Code 307.106).

Routine lawn and landscape care is exempt, but new hardscape isn't (Ord. Code 307.107), and turf sits on a compacted stone base the code doesn't classify. The City's Historic Preservation Section runs the certificate process and can approve applications that meet its administrative criteria (Riverside Avondale Preservation). Ask it two things: does this need a certificate, and can staff approve it?

blocks.h2: The district's guidelines are written from the sidewalk.
blocks.takeaway: A front-yard turf lawn is the likeliest to get a closer look from the City. On most interior lots, the large back yard sits out of the sidewalk's view.
paras: The City's August 1997 guidelines tie the certificate to changes seen from a public right-of-way, and list landscaping among the changes staff or the Commission may give a non-binding opinion on (Guidelines, Part 1). The code has been amended since, so treat that as intent, not a ruling.

They picture the front yard as small, with the house close to the sidewalk and a grass lawn crossed by a straight concrete or hexagonal-paver walk, and they ask that new plantings, fencing and walks fit the neighborhood in size, scale, materials and color (Guidelines, Part 2). A turf front lawn is the likeliest to get a closer look. The large back yard sits out of that view on most interior lots, which makes it the easier place for a lawn or a small putting green.

The guidelines also warn against removing historic walkways, fencing or trees before their importance is weighed, and ask that the rock-faced cast concrete retaining walls common here be kept. We cut the turf to meet them.

blocks.h2: Put the dog run behind a six-foot fence and it drops out of the street's view.
blocks.takeaway: On an interior lot, a dog run behind a six-foot fence starting behind the house's front wall is out of the street's sight. Corner lots are held to four feet on both street sides.
paras: Under fencing guidelines the Historic Preservation Commission adopted on 26 February 2003, a fence that follows them can be approved by staff (Fencing Guidelines). Back-yard fences go to six feet and front-yard fences to four, and a fence over four feet has to sit at least 20 feet back from the right-of-way of the primary front yard.

On an interior lot, pet turf behind a six-foot fence that starts behind the front wall of the house is out of the street's sight. A corner lot's two street sides are both held to four feet, so a side-yard run stays in view. If the run needs a new fence, put the fence and the turf in one request.

blocks.h2: Staff approval takes a site plan and photos. A hearing takes signs and weeks.
blocks.takeaway: Staff review asks for a site plan and street photos, and the layout we draw after the free visit marks the turf's footprint. A Commission hearing needs your application filed at least 21 days ahead.
paras: For staff review, the 1997 guidelines ask for a site plan with the change marked on it, photos of the house from the street, and sometimes a sample or manufacturer's description of the material. The custom layout we draw after the free visit marks the turf's footprint and edges.

Applications staff can't approve go to a Commission hearing. The completed application has to be filed at least 21 calendar days before the meeting, you post signs no more than 200 feet apart on every street side at least 14 days before it, and the Commission decides within 30 days of the hearing (307.106). A staff decision can be appealed within 21 days, by you or anyone with standing (307.107). A certificate expires if work hasn't started within 12 months, or isn't finished within five years unless the Commission extends it.

blocks.h2: Riverside's soil holds water near the surface. Avondale's lets it go.
blocks.takeaway: Near Five Points the soil holds water about a foot down, while Avondale's drains better, and either can turn up old fill. The base must drain, with no pooling or added runoff next door.
paras: USDA soil mapping splits the district. Near Five Points it's Urban land-Mascotte-Sapelo complex, 0 to 2 percent slopes, with both named soils rated poorly drained and a wet layer about 31 centimetres down, roughly a foot (USDA). In Avondale around St. Johns Avenue it's Urban land-Ortega-Kershaw complex, 0 to 8 percent slopes, where Ortega's wet layer sits about 147 centimetres down and Kershaw is excessively drained. In both, 35 percent is mapped as urban land rather than a named soil, so a dig can turn up old fill.

At the Riverside end, the base has to carry water off: the state standard requires a subgrade prepared for positive drainage, with no pooling and no added runoff onto a neighbor's lot (Rule 62-308.100), and the district guidelines want site drainage kept from running toward the house's foundation. Watering days and the 2026 shortage order are on our Jacksonville page.

servicesNote: Choose a lawn, a fenced dog run or a courtyard putting green, and decide early which parts of it the street will see.

faq.q: Who installs artificial turf in Riverside Avondale, Jacksonville?
faq.a: We install artificial lawns, pet turf and backyard putting greens in Riverside and Avondale, starting with a free visit to measure and check the ground, then a custom layout you approve. Riverside Avondale Preservation's free videos show how to check whether your home is inside the historic district. Call 303-349-2368 for a free estimate.

faq.q: Doesn't Florida law stop the City from refusing turf?
faq.a: It limits the City on some lots. On a single-family property of an acre or less, a local government may not adopt or enforce a rule that prohibits turf meeting the state standard (Fla. Stat. 125.572). The statute doesn't mention historic districts. DEP says local governments may still regulate within the standard, which doesn't reach duplexes, condominiums or commercial property, and sends anyone who sees a conflict to the local government or legal counsel (DEP).

faq.q: Can turf go where I park out front?
faq.a: Not as parking. In the overlay's Historic Residential Character Area, the part not placed in a commercial, office, industrial or urban transition area (656.399.19), front-yard parking is prohibited except in a designated driveway, and so is parking between the street edge and the sidewalk (656.399.25). Plan turf around the driveway, not as a pad beside it.

faq.q: Does Riverside Avondale Preservation approve my plans?
faq.a: No. It's a nonprofit that posts the City's guidelines and explains the process, and it says it has no final decision-making power. Decisions come from City staff or the Jacksonville Historic Preservation Commission, whose seven members are appointed by the Mayor.
